narrative:
The model estimated a 56.7% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. Because that is above 50%, the application was denied: the decision reflects a modestly higher predicted risk, not a certainty or a judgment about your ability.

The strongest factor was your third-year class rank. You were in the second decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile; this low relative standing was the main reason the prediction moved toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor. At 39, it was above the accepted-student average of about 37, so it pushed toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA was third. At 3.10, it was slightly below the accepted average of 3.23, but its overall influence still leaned modestly toward passing. Those positives were not enough to offset the concern about your third-year academic standing. Gender and race were not used.

Next, focus on demonstrating stronger recent academic readiness, especially in upper-level law-related coursework. Consider post-baccalaureate or graduate study, an academic-enhancement program, or retaking relevant courses if possible. If illness, work, or other circumstances affected your third-year grades, provide a brief explanation. Seek admissions advising, strengthen the rest of your application, and reapply to schools where your profile fits. Your LSAT is a relative strength, so prioritize academic improvement over retaking it unless an advisor recommends otherwise.
